segments.voice: Yesterday, the Brahmanda, and two tellings of Sita, both agreeing she is never Ravana's. Today a new run begins: a fish, a tortoise, a boar, and why a row of animals is one god.

Avatar, these days, is a profile picture or a character in a game. It's Sanskrit first. On some calendar prints and temple walls there's a row of pictures: a fish, a tortoise, a boar, a figure with a lion's head, a small boy with an umbrella, and on down the row. Every one of them is Vishnu. And there's an old song that walks along that row, with a refrain that keeps coming back after every verse: jaya jagadisha hare. Today is about that sound, and the row it holds together.

segments.voice: Avatara means a descent, a coming down. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says, in paraphrase, that whenever dharma fails and wrong rises, he comes, age after age, to protect the good and set things right. The Puranas tell those comings as stories, and one list of ten became a series: Matsya the fish, Kurma the tortoise, Varaha the boar, Narasimha the man-lion, Vamana the dwarf, Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, the Buddha in some lists and Balarama in others, and Kalki, still to come. The lists don't all agree; the Bhagavata Purana names more than ten. Now the sound. In the Gita Govinda, the poet Jayadeva sings a hymn to the ten. Each verse names one descent and ends the same way: jaya jagadisha hare, victory, Hari, lord of the world. The shapes change, verse after verse. The refrain doesn't. That's the series in one sound: a fish in the flood, a boar under the earth, a prince with a bow, the same one coming down in whatever shape that age's trouble calls for. Some readers see a pattern in the order, from water to land to the human world; others take each descent on its own. Either way, the row starts in the water, with a fish.

segments.voice: Pick one sound that keeps coming back where you are: a clock, a fan, traffic outside, your own breath. Each time it returns, notice it's the same sound in a new moment, like a refrain after a new verse. If you pray, you can let the refrain run quietly under your breath: jaya jagadisha hare.
The ten avatars as a series: Vishnu's descents, read as one row, held together like verses by a refrain.
